holocene.title: Holocene
holocene.subtitle: 12,000 years ago to Present · The Age of Humanity
holocene.body:
The Holocene is a warm interglacial period marked by retreating glaciers and rising sea levels. Stable climates allowed diverse ecosystems to flourish across the continents.

During this epoch, Ice Age megafauna vanished while humans rapidly expanded, developing agriculture and complex civilizations that reshaped modern Earth.

mid_pleistocene.title: Mid Pleistocene
mid_pleistocene.subtitle: ~1 Ma · Ice Ages and Giants
mid_pleistocene.body:
The Mid Pleistocene is defined by intensifying ice ages with longer, colder glacial cycles. Massive ice sheets repeatedly advanced, drastically lowering global sea levels.

Large cold-adapted megafauna thrived across vast steppes and tundras. Meanwhile, early human species expanded across the Old World, adapting through stone tools.

early_quaternary.title: Early Quaternary
early_quaternary.subtitle: ~2 Ma · Dawn of the Ice Age
early_quaternary.body:
The Early Quaternary marked the start of cyclical ice ages as permanent ice sheets locked onto the poles and global temperatures plummeted.

Grasslands spread worldwide, supporting diverse large mammals. In Africa, early human ancestors emerged, crafted primitive tools, and began their global expansion.

late_neogene.title: Late Neogene
late_neogene.subtitle: ~5 Ma · The Cooling World
late_neogene.body:
The Late Neogene experienced ongoing global cooling and drying. Shifting landmasses reorganized ocean currents, and widespread grasslands replaced dense ancient forests.

Grazing mammals diversified rapidly to exploit the open plains. In Africa, early bipedal hominins arose as modern ecosystems began taking shape.

mid_neogene.title: Mid Neogene
mid_neogene.subtitle: ~15 Ma · The Miocene Climatic Optimum
mid_neogene.body:
The Mid Neogene was a warm interval known as the Miocene Climatic Optimum, where lush forests extended toward the poles.

Apes diversified across Africa and Eurasia while marine mammals flourished in the seas. Open grasslands and modern mountain chains gradually emerged.

early_neogene.title: Early Neogene
early_neogene.subtitle: ~20 Ma · A World Without Grass
early_neogene.body:
The Early Neogene was a warm, heavily forested world before the widespread dominance of grasslands. Modern continental layouts were gradually assembling.

Primitive mammals such as early horses and mastodons spread across the land, while diverse apes flourished in warm tropical forests.

late_paleogene.title: Late Paleogene
late_paleogene.subtitle: ~35 Ma · The Great Cooling
late_paleogene.body:
The Late Paleogene saw dramatic global cooling as Antarctica became isolated by ocean currents, sparking the growth of massive continental ice.

Warm tropical jungles retreated toward the equator, giving way to open woodlands and the earliest grasslands where modern mammal lineages diversified.

mid_paleogene.title: Mid Paleogene
mid_paleogene.subtitle: ~50 Ma · The Warm Eocene World
mid_paleogene.body:
The Mid Paleogene was an intensely warm greenhouse epoch, with lush subtropical forests and warm wetlands stretching as far as polar regions.

Mammals diversified rapidly to fill vacated ecological niches. Early ancestors of modern horses, primates, and whales made their initial appearances.

early_paleogene.title: Early Paleogene
early_paleogene.subtitle: ~60 Ma · Mammals Inherit the Earth
early_paleogene.body:
The Early Paleogene was a period of rapid evolutionary recovery following the catastrophic extinction of the non-avian dinosaurs.

Once small and nocturnal, mammals quickly diversified into larger forms across warm, forested continents alongside large predatory flightless birds.

late_cretaceous.title: Late Cretaceous
late_cretaceous.subtitle: ~75 Ma · The Dinosaur Dynasties
late_cretaceous.body:
The Late Cretaceous represented the magnificent final peak of dinosaur diversity in a warm, greenhouse world divided by shallow inland seas.

Flowering plants transformed terrestrial landscapes, while giant predators ruled on land and massive marine reptiles dominated the warm global oceans.

mid_cretaceous.title: Mid Cretaceous
mid_cretaceous.subtitle: ~100 Ma · The Greenhouse Peak
mid_cretaceous.body:
The Mid Cretaceous was an extreme greenhouse epoch characterized by soaring global temperatures, high sea levels, and ice-free poles.

Vast inland seas deposited thick chalk beds, while giant carnivorous dinosaurs roamed landmasses reshaped by the earliest flowering plants.

early_cretaceous.title: Early Cretaceous
early_cretaceous.subtitle: ~130 Ma · Feathers and Flowers
early_cretaceous.body:
The Early Cretaceous was a transformative interval as the supercontinent Gondwana fragmented and flowering plants began their global evolutionary spread.

Feathered dinosaurs flourished in astonishing diversity alongside early birds, while giant sauropods and predatory dinosaurs dominated terrestrial biomes.

late_jurassic.title: Late Jurassic
late_jurassic.subtitle: ~150 Ma · The Age of Giants
late_jurassic.body:
The Late Jurassic was the iconic age of giants, marked by massive sauropods and apex predators dominating lush, warm landscapes.

Conifer forests covered rifting continents, early birds began taking flight, and warm shallow seas teemed with diverse marine reptiles and sharks.

mid_jurassic.title: Mid Jurassic
mid_jurassic.subtitle: ~165 Ma · Dinosaurs Rise to Dominance
mid_jurassic.body:
The Mid Jurassic saw dinosaurs firmly establish their dominance as the supercontinent Pangaea divided into northern Laurasia and southern Gondwana.

Giant long-necked herbivores and armored dinosaurs multiplied across dense conifer forests, while ancient coral reefs expanded across warm marine basins.

early_jurassic.title: Early Jurassic
early_jurassic.subtitle: ~195 Ma · Life After the Great Dying
early_jurassic.body:
The Early Jurassic was a time of recovery following a devastating mass extinction that eliminated most competing terrestrial reptiles.

Dinosaurs rapidly diversified into newly vacant ecological niches, while the supercontinent Pangaea began rifting to create the early Atlantic Ocean.

late_triassic.title: Late Triassic
late_triassic.subtitle: ~215 Ma · The Rise of the Dinosaurs
late_triassic.body:
The Late Triassic featured the assembled supercontinent of Pangaea, where early dinosaurs competed against large crocodile-like archosaurs across arid landscapes.

The first true mammals and flying pterosaurs emerged during this period, just before massive volcanism triggered another major mass extinction.

mid_triassic.title: Mid Triassic
mid_triassic.subtitle: ~235 Ma · Recovery and Radiation
mid_triassic.body:
The Mid Triassic was an active recovery phase following Earth’s worst mass extinction, with life gradually rebuilding complex ecological networks.

Archosaurs flourished and gave rise to the first true dinosaurs, while newly evolved marine reptiles rapidly colonized warm coastal waters.

early_triassic.title: Early Triassic
early_triassic.subtitle: ~245 Ma · The Aftermath of Annihilation
early_triassic.body:
The Early Triassic was a harsh, impoverished aftermath to the Great Dying, with extreme heat and toxic oceans slowing ecological recovery.

A few resilient survivor species, notably the burrowing therapsid Lystrosaurus, dominated barren terrestrial environments before biological diversity slowly rebounded.

late_permian.title: Late Permian
late_permian.subtitle: ~260 Ma · Before the Great Dying
late_permian.body:
The Late Permian featured a fully assembled Pangaea containing vast arid interiors and lush coastal forests populated by complex animal communities.

Diverse mammal-like therapsids and massive herbivorous reptiles ruled the land, flourishing just before cataclysmic volcanism triggered life’s greatest extinction.

mid_permian.title: Mid Permian
mid_permian.subtitle: ~275 Ma · Therapsids Take Over
mid_permian.body:
The Mid Permian marked a major vertebrate transition as primitive pelycosaurs were replaced by advanced mammal-like therapsids across drying continents.

Large herbivores and fierce carnivores thrived across Pangaea, while southern swamp forests laid down extensive coal deposits in a cooling climate.

early_permian.title: Early Permian
early_permian.subtitle: ~290 Ma · Pangaea Takes Shape
early_permian.body:
The Early Permian witnessed the final assembly of Pangaea, raising mighty mountain ranges and drying out vast portions of the continental interior.

Egg-laying amniotes diversified away from water, with sail-backed pelycosaurs becoming the dominant land predators as ancient swamp forests receded.

late_carboniferous.title: Late Carboniferous
late_carboniferous.subtitle: ~305 Ma · The Coal Age
late_carboniferous.body:
The Late Carboniferous was dominated by sprawling tropical coal swamps fueled by towering lycopsid trees and exceptionally high atmospheric oxygen.

Giant flying insects and massive arthropods thrived in the dense canopies, while early reptiles began moving away from watery wetlands.

mid_carboniferous.title: Mid Carboniferous
mid_carboniferous.subtitle: ~320 Ma · Giants of the Coal Forests
mid_carboniferous.body:
The Mid Carboniferous was blanketed in colossal swamp forests that accumulated massive peat layers, ultimately forming the world’s major coal seams.

Amphibians ruled freshwater habitats, while the earliest reptiles evolved hard-shelled eggs that freed terrestrial vertebrates from reproducing in water.

early_carboniferous.title: Early Carboniferous
early_carboniferous.subtitle: ~345 Ma · A World Turned Green
early_carboniferous.body:
The Early Carboniferous saw the widespread expansion of early forests across continental lowlands, driving a major drawdown of atmospheric carbon dioxide.

Amphibians became the leading land vertebrates in newly green landscapes, while diverse sharks and marine invertebrates populated warm, shallow seas.

late_devonian.title: Late Devonian
late_devonian.subtitle: ~370 Ma · When Fish Grew Legs
late_devonian.body:
The Late Devonian witnessed the historic transition of vertebrates from water to land as lobe-finned fish evolved limb-like fins.

Pioneering amphibians explored early terrestrial forests, while formidable armored placoderms continued to rule the oceans before a looming extinction crisis.

mid_devonian.title: Mid Devonian
mid_devonian.subtitle: ~390 Ma · The Age of Fishes
mid_devonian.body:
The Mid Devonian was the heart of the Age of Fishes, with armored placoderms and early sharks dominating marine ecosystems.

On land, the first true forests emerged as primitive woody trees and arthropods began establishing complex terrestrial environments.

early_devonian.title: Early Devonian
early_devonian.subtitle: ~410 Ma · Plants Conquer the Land
early_devonian.body:
The Early Devonian launched a terrestrial revolution as simple vascular plants spread inland, creating organic soils and stabilizing riverbanks.

Early arthropods followed plant life onto dry land, while jawed fish and sprawling coral reefs multiplied rapidly throughout the oceans.

late_silurian.title: Late Silurian
late_silurian.subtitle: ~420 Ma · Ancient Seas and Shore Life
late_silurian.body:
The Late Silurian featured warm, reef-fringed oceans dominated by giant sea scorpions, trilobites, and diversifying early jawed fish.

Along damp coastlines, the earliest vascular plants and primitive arthropods took root, initiating the gradual colonization of dry land.

mid_silurian.title: Mid Silurian
mid_silurian.subtitle: ~430 Ma · Reefs and Sea Scorpions
mid_silurian.body:
The Mid Silurian was a period of marine recovery where ancient coral reefs rebuilt complex habitats across warm, tropical shelf seas.

Predatory sea scorpions and jawless fish ruled the coastal waters, while tiny primitive plants established early footholds along damp shorelines.

early_silurian.title: Early Silurian
early_silurian.subtitle: ~440 Ma · Recovery After Extinction
early_silurian.body:
The Early Silurian marked the gradual return of marine life after the catastrophic end-Ordovician glaciation wiped out most oceanic species.

Surviving invertebrates and jawless fish recolonized rebounding shelf seas, while land surfaces remained largely barren except for simple coastal crusts.

late_ordovician.title: Late Ordovician
late_ordovician.subtitle: ~450 Ma · Ocean World
late_ordovician.body:
The Late Ordovician was an ocean-dominated world harboring exceptionally diverse marine life, led by giant predatory cephalopods, trilobites, and extensive shell beds.

Continents remained largely barren rock, and the period ended abruptly when massive southern polar glaciation triggered a devastating global extinction.

mid_ordovician.title: Mid Ordovician
mid_ordovician.subtitle: ~465 Ma · The Great Biodiversification
mid_ordovician.body:
The Mid Ordovician was defined by an explosion of marine diversity that dramatically expanded invertebrate families across warm, shallow seas.

The first coral reefs arose, nautiloid cephalopods became top predators, and life began building complex, multi-layered seafloor communities.

early_ordovician.title: Early Ordovician
early_ordovician.subtitle: ~480 Ma · Ancient Seas of Life
early_ordovician.body:
The Early Ordovician built upon the anatomical innovations of the Cambrian, setting off an accelerating radiation of marine invertebrate life.

Trilobites and early cephalopods thrived across high-sea-level oceans, while dry land surfaces remained largely devoid of complex multicellular organisms.

late_cambrian.title: Late Cambrian
late_cambrian.subtitle: ~495 Ma · Trilobite Seas
late_cambrian.body:
The Late Cambrian was characterized by warm, expansive shallow seas dominated by an extraordinary variety of specialized trilobite species.

Early jawless vertebrates swam among primitive molluscs and echinoderms, despite periodic extinction pulses that repeatedly reshuffled marine ecosystems.

mid_cambrian.title: Mid Cambrian
mid_cambrian.subtitle: ~510 Ma · The Burgess Shale World
mid_cambrian.body:
The Mid Cambrian is famous for the bizarre marine fauna preserved in extraordinary fossil sites like the Burgess Shale.

Apex predators like Anomalocaris hunted among diverse trilobites and early chordates, establishing the fundamental body plans of modern animals.

early_cambrian.title: Early Cambrian
early_cambrian.subtitle: ~530 Ma · The Dawn of Complex Life
early_cambrian.body:
The Early Cambrian marked the sudden dawn of complex animal life, with creatures rapidly developing mineralized shells, limbs, and compound eyes.

An intense evolutionary arms race between predators and prey transformed quiet ocean floors into dynamic, modern-style marine ecosystems.

cambrian_explosion.title: The Cambrian Explosion
cambrian_explosion.subtitle: 538 Ma · When Animals Invented Themselves
cambrian_explosion.body:
The Cambrian Explosion was a rapid evolutionary leap in which nearly all modern animal body plans first emerged in the fossil record.

Within a geologically brief window, animals evolved hard shells, eyes, and predatory behaviors, permanently transforming life on Earth.

great_ordovician_biodiversification.title: Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event
great_ordovician_biodiversification.subtitle: 470 Ma · Life's Greatest Marine Expansion
great_ordovician_biodiversification.body:
The Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event was a monumental expansion of marine life, multiplying animal species within established Cambrian lineages.

Invertebrates constructed the first true coral reefs and complex seafloor ecosystems, establishing ecological patterns that lasted for hundreds of millions of years.

end_ordovician_extinction.title: End-Ordovician Mass Extinction
end_ordovician_extinction.subtitle: 443 Ma · Ice, Anoxia, and Annihilation
end_ordovician_extinction.body:
The End-Ordovician Mass Extinction wiped out roughly eighty-five percent of marine species through two devastating pulses of intense southern polar glaciation.

Crashing sea levels destroyed shallow habitats, followed by deadly, oxygen-starved waters as glaciers melted and flooded continental shelves.

late_devonian_extinction.title: Late Devonian Mass Extinction
late_devonian_extinction.subtitle: 374 Ma · The Kelwasser Event
late_devonian_extinction.body:
The Late Devonian Mass Extinction decimated ancient coral reef systems and marine life through prolonged ocean cooling and widespread oxygen depletion.

Rapidly expanding land plants and volcanic activity likely triggered the crisis, though early land-dwelling vertebrates managed to survive and flourish.

carboniferous_rainforest_collapse.title: Carboniferous Rainforest Collapse
carboniferous_rainforest_collapse.subtitle: 307 Ma · When the Coal Forests Fell
carboniferous_rainforest_collapse.body:
The Carboniferous Rainforest Collapse occurred when climate cooling and drying fragmented the vast equatorial coal swamps into isolated patches.

While giant swamp-dwelling amphibians and insects declined, egg-laying reptiles thrived in the open landscapes, sparking their rise to terrestrial dominance.

permian_triassic_extinction.title: Permian-Triassic Mass Extinction
permian_triassic_extinction.subtitle: 252 Ma · The Great Dying
permian_triassic_extinction.body:
The Permian-Triassic Mass Extinction, or Great Dying, was Earth’s most catastrophic extinction, eradicating over ninety percent of all species.

Massive volcanic eruptions in Siberia triggered runaway global warming, acid rain, and ocean suffocation, driving global ecosystems to the brink of collapse.

triassic_jurassic_extinction.title: Triassic-Jurassic Mass Extinction
triassic_jurassic_extinction.subtitle: 201 Ma · The Extinction That Made the Dinosaurs
triassic_jurassic_extinction.body:
The Triassic-Jurassic Mass Extinction eliminated roughly eighty percent of species, driven by massive volcanic eruptions as Pangaea began rifting apart.

The catastrophe wiped out large archosaurs and amphibians, clearing the ecological stage for dinosaurs to become the uncontested rulers of the planet.

jurassic_marine_revolution.title: Mesozoic Marine Revolution
jurassic_marine_revolution.subtitle: 155 Ma · An Arms Race Beneath the Waves
jurassic_marine_revolution.body:
The Mesozoic Marine Revolution was a prolonged evolutionary arms race where new shell-crushing predators forced marine prey to adapt rapidly.

Molluscs evolved thicker armor and burrowed into seafloor sediment, fundamentally transforming ancient ocean floors into modern, highly interactive ecosystems.

kpg_extinction.title: K-Pg Mass Extinction
kpg_extinction.subtitle: 66 Ma · The Day the Dinosaurs Died
kpg_extinction.body:
The K-Pg Mass Extinction occurred when a massive asteroid impact triggered global wildfires, darkness, and severe cooling that collapsed global food chains.

Non-avian dinosaurs and giant marine reptiles vanished completely, allowing surviving birds and small mammals to inherit and reshape the planet.

petm.title: Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum
petm.subtitle: 56 Ma · Earth Overheats
petm.body:
The Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum was an extreme, rapid warming event caused by a massive surge of carbon into the atmosphere and oceans.

Soaring temperatures acidified oceans and drove evolutionary shifts on land, spurring the early radiation of modern mammalian orders like primates.

eocene_oligocene_transition.title: Eocene-Oligocene Transition
eocene_oligocene_transition.subtitle: 34 Ma · The Big Chill
eocene_oligocene_transition.body:
The Eocene-Oligocene Transition plunged Earth into a cooler climate as new ocean currents isolated Antarctica, locking it under massive permanent ice sheets.

Dense subtropical forests retreated globally, paving the way for open woodlands, expanding grasslands, and the rise of modern grazing mammals.
